opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, testing turned out to be one of the most interesting parts of it. In SWE-bench, the model never sees the hidden tests used for grading. It just gets the issue description and the repo, and at the end its patch is checked against tests it never saw. So the model can't really "test" in the sense of running the official suite and iterating until it's green.

What we saw work well is the model behaving like a good engineer. Before touching anything, it reads the issue and writes a small reproduction script that triggers the bug. Then it runs that, confirms it actually sees the failure, makes the fix, and reruns the script to confirm the behavior changed. That loop of reproducing, fixing, and verifying made a big difference, because it grounds the model in the real behavior of the code instead of what it imagines the code does.

We also encouraged it to think about edge cases. Once the obvious repro passes, it should ask what nearby inputs might break, since the hidden tests often check exactly those. Models that stopped at "my one example works" left a lot of points on the table.

There's a subtlety too. You don't want the model rewriting existing tests to make them pass, or overfitting to its own little script. Its own tests are a tool for building confidence, not the objective. The objective is resolving the issue the way a maintainer would want.

So I'd say testing is less about a pass/fail signal and more about giving the model a feedback loop with reality. The more the agent can run code and observe what actually happens, the less it hallucinates fixes, and that was probably one of the biggest levers we found.

r001.rationale: It says the model never sees the hidden grading tests, but does not explain that this is to prevent tailoring its solution to those tests.

r002.rationale: It describes writing a reproduction script, running it to confirm the bug, then rerunning it after the fix to verify the behavior changed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think testing is actually the thing that makes SWE-bench tractable at all for a model. If you just handed a model a GitHub issue and a repo and said "fix this, no feedback," you'd get something that looks plausible but is wrong a huge fraction of the time. What makes the agentic setup work is that the model can write a change and then actually check it, and that loop is where most of the value comes from.

The way I think about it, a good coding model treats tests the way a good engineer does. The first thing you do when you land on a bug is reproduce it. So the model should write a small script or a test case that fails in the way the issue describes, before it touches any code. That does two things. It confirms the model actually understands the problem, and it gives you a signal you can trust later, because when that script passes, you know you've changed the behavior and not just something adjacent to it.

Then there's the existing test suite, which is really a regression guard. A lot of SWE-bench failures aren't "the model couldn't fix the bug," they're "the model fixed the bug and broke three other things." The hidden tests in the benchmark include tests that were already passing, so if you're not running the relevant parts of the suite you'll get burned. The model has to be smart about scope there, because these repos can have test suites that take a very long time, so it should figure out which tests touch the files it changed and run those.

One thing I'd caution against is treating tests as the goal rather than as evidence. It's really easy for a model to learn to overfit to its own test, or worse, to modify a failing test so it passes. That's the behavior you absolutely don't want, and it's something we pay a lot of attention to in training. The test should be checking the behavior the issue asks for, and the model should be skeptical of its own fix until it's actually seen the failure go away for the right reason.

And honestly, the limitation is that the model can only test what it thinks to test. The hidden tests in SWE-bench sometimes cover edge cases the model never considered. So part of what you're measuring is not just "can you write code," it's "can you reason about what a careful maintainer would want to verify." That's a judgment skill, and testing is the mechanism that lets the model exercise it rather than just guess.

r001.rationale: The response says SWE-bench has hidden tests and notes they may cover overlooked edge cases, but it does not explain that grading tests are hidden to prevent the model from tailoring its solution to them.

r002.rationale: It recommends writing a script or test that reproduces the bug before changing code and says it can later show the behavior changed. It does not clearly say the model repeatedly reruns that script during the task.

astra-6.text:
I think testing is really the feedback loop that lets a coding model go from making a plausible change to knowing whether that change actually works. On a SWE-bench task, you have an issue description and a repository, but the issue usually isn’t a complete specification. So you want the model to reproduce the problem, make a change, and then run tests to see whether it fixed the problem and whether it broke anything else.

The subtle part is that passing tests isn’t the same as being correct. If the model writes its own test, it can encode the same misunderstanding in both the test and the implementation. So you want it to use the existing tests, reason about what the issue is asking for, and add a regression test that actually distinguishes the broken behavior from the intended behavior. The value is in that iterative process, rather than just running a test suite once at the end.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that SWE-bench grading tests are hidden or explain that this prevents tailoring a solution to them.

r002.rationale: It discusses reproducing the problem and iterative testing, but does not describe using a script that reproduces the reported bug and repeatedly rerunning that script.

sol-6.1.text:
I think testing is really the feedback loop that lets a coding model move beyond just proposing a plausible patch. It can make a change, run the relevant tests, look at the failure, and revise its approach. That’s a much more powerful way to work than trying to get everything right in one shot.

But the tests are also an incomplete specification. Passing the tests you can see doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve solved the issue. You still need to understand the intended behavior, check that the change actually addresses it, and make sure you haven’t broken something else. Ideally, the model can write a regression test that fails before the fix and passes afterward. That gives it much stronger evidence that it’s making progress.

r001.rationale: The response discusses tests as an incomplete specification but does not say SWE-bench hides grading tests or explain that this prevents tailoring.
